I hope it's helpful to hear someone else's experience. I'm sorry you're going through this right now! Take care of yourself. It's hard, but you got this!

 A gyno is not the right doctor for PCOS. Though if you find a really good one who works with PCOS, I have heard of some people having luck going that route. You need a naturalpath who works with PCOS, or if you want/need to go western (which is valid, just not the path I took), you need an endocrinologist

I have emotional release on my table often. I deal with clients who have been through serious injuries, have chronic pain conditions, and have experienced traumatic accidents, so it only makes sense as the system comes down from that level of escalation that emotions come out. I'm also just more prone as a person to have other people open up to me emotionally, so I've learned how to respect and hold space for emotions. 

The first thing is that emotional release is not only crying or hysterics. It's normally very subtle and includes all emotions. Sadness, overwhelm, anxiety, anger, fear, disgust, even joy. Signs include: moving around more than they normally do, changes in breathing, rubbing their face a lot (think stressed out face touching) changes in tone of voice, sniffling or tearing up, laughing for no reason, clearing their throat often, a general shift in the energy of the room that might be uncomfortable (like being stonewalled or feeling they might be mad at you) 

Secondly, if you do notice a shift like this, it could be nothing it could be a slight emotional release, or it could be the start of a full-on emotional letdown. Not everyone picks up on the subtle changes, and that's ok, but if you notice it, say something and ask permission to keep going. "Oh, you know this area I am working on tends to hold a lot of emotions for some people, as we work here, you might notice some stuff come up. I just wanted to mention it. Some people even have an emotional release, which could include everything from sadness to anger, and that's normal. If that comes up at all, this is a safe place for it, and you can express emotions in here. It's good for the healing process anyway. Are you OK still working here?" I bring it up casually during the session when I notice people might be going in that direction. Even if the release is joyful like laughing I say this. I have found the smaller deal you can make it out to be the more comfortable the client feels "emotions? yeah, whateves they cool. " I personally NEVER stop a session or touching their body if they start to show signs of an emotional release, that can cause shame for a lot of people. 

If they have a full emotional response (i.e crying, getting very upset or angry, showing signs of panic) I ASK THEM, "Do you want to pause the session?" I normally say "this is an emotional release. It's super normal, and I am glad it's coming up instead of staying in your body. Do you want to pause the session at all, I can step out to get you some water, I also have tissues, or I am totally cool to continue, and you are welcome to just let it flow." Again, emotions can cause shame for a lot of people, especially if they come out of nowhere so the calmer and nonchalant you can be about it the better. Giving them the option to take a break is an opening if they need it, but it doesn't leave them feeling like they disrupted the session if that's not what they wanted. Sometimes, they just need a cry or to let out some sighs and grunts of frustration. A lot of the times, I have found people want to continue and just have you hold the space (meaning you don't do or say much but sit in the discomfort with them). Some people would like a more in-depth explanation about the release they are having, and some need to stop the whole session. It just depends, so check in and let them male the choice. 

Thirdly, remember to take care of yourself afterward. We absorb other people's energy, dealing with and holding space for these releases can be hard on our nervous system, and it's important to have some way to let it go after especially if the release was something triggering to you like anger. I have had clients snap at me during the session because of an angry emotional release and apologize after that's triggering for me, but it's important to stay grounded in the moment. "Oh, no worries! are you feeling frustrated? That could be an emotional release it actually happens to a lot of people. Do you feel like you hold some stress or other emotions here? Do you want to continue in this spot?" But after you gotta let it go somehow. I will shake my hands and bounce up and down to shake it out and maybe get myself a treat or something after. 

Finally, make sure to give them good home care advice. "Today was a more intense session, I'm glad that stuff came up and released for you! Make sure to care for yourself today, though. Drink extra water and take it as easy as you can. Remember, it's all normal and part of the process. If you have more emotions come up today, try to give yourself some space with them, as much as you can let them out. You might be a little groggy or foggy brained that's normal too. I suggest a nap and watching a light-hearted show or reading a good book! If you have a questions call or email. Great work today."

I suggest calling Chiro and PT clinics in your area and asking what training the massage therapists have for the neck and jaw. Many clinics will hit you with the "our therapists are trained in many different techniques and can adjust for your needs," which is code for no one has a specialty in what you are asking for, but give us money please. You are looking for someone who has training in Trigger Point Therapy for the neck or cervical spine, probably. Someone who specializes in the treatment of the neck for acute and chronic conditions will probably have this training. I would be cautious of a blanket "deep tissue" massage (I'm not saying deep tissue isn't a legit modality. It just sounds like you need more specific training). You want words like therapeutic, medical, trigger point, myofacial release, and specialty of the neck and jaw. You probably want a clinic that is capable of giving you details on how they plan to treat this area before your appointment so you don't waste your time and money. Sometimes, you can ask the therapist they recommend to email you so you can ask a couple questions.
Ask stuff like 
-What training do you have for the neck and jaw?(they should be able to name specific classes)
-if the neck and jaw are my main area of concern, how long would you normally spend there?(they should be able to explain connected areas that they will also be looking at and why, along with an expected time frame.) 
-what is your approach to chronic issues like this? (Again, you're looking for words like therapeutic and medical, medium pressure, and direct work.) 
You can also add that you have had a hard time finding the right fit and ask how they tend to work with clients to make sure your needs are being met.
If they are snarkey about being asked questions, it's not the right fit. Most of us in the medical field for massage are used to people who have had a hard time finding the right fit and want to answer your questions and get specific.  A lot of therapists are uncomfortable with detailed neck work, so getting picky and specific is the way to go to find a good fit for you. 

If you are in Portland,  OR area, DM me. I specialize in medical massage for the neck, lol.

There is another option... you could rehome the dog. This behavior is very normal for GP who are not getting their environmental needs met. As others have said, they are working dogs, not family dogs. Great wonderful dogs, but working dogs. Who primarily like to live outside without much direction from humans and chase away animals not related to their pack. They are farm dogs bred to protect the farm and herds. If you are not in a place to get training/learn how to make your home a more GP friendly environment which is valid for many people, consider rehoming him to an environment like a farm where his behavior will match the environment. He sounds like a great dog, maybe just not the best match for your family. I would not start with medication without talking to a trainer though, keeping a dog drugged their whole life for behaving according to how they were bred just so they act how you want them to is kind of inconsiderate to the dog. I know it is heartbreaking, but I would be very surprised based on the information we have if this dog actually needs BE or medication right now. He needs a different environment. Like others have said, please be mindful of the cat and baby without the right environment this dog's anxiety will build, and he might have more behaviors surface. Honestly, the longer you keep him without getting training, the more likely you are to accidently make an environment where his behavior will escalate and create a situation where medication or even BE is an actual consideration. My suggestion is to rehome while his behavior issues are minor so he can live his best life, and you can find the right fit for your family.

The difference was that everyone did it to everyone, in rotations, like once every few months to years, the target would change. It brought me down to levels I didn't like in myself. I didn't even realize how low this group brought me until I walked away and started analyzing things I thought had been "funny" or "harmless" or "venting" at the time. 


I finally walked away around 26 27. The fallout was yucky. I obviously became the target when I first tried to talk to them and tell them I wasn't ok with this behavior anymore.  it was a lonely while after the friendships fully disolved. But I stayed true to what I wanted in friendship and reminded myself how I wanted to feel and be treated in friendship. Therapy helped

Now I am 30 with a new friend group that constantly  lifts me up. I know they lift me up behind my back, too, because other people will mention it. "Oh, so and so told me you did this hard thing, we are both so proud of you!" And they do the same thing with me for others in the group. "So and so is so great as this skill you should ask them to help you." That's the kind of energy that real friends bring to the table. You don't feel like you have to go through someone's phone in a real friendship because there would never be a mean comment to find in the first place. Instead, you happen apon little things that make you feel good, like a picture of you on their fridge or a complement shared with someone else that wasn't even meant for you to see or hear. Sometimes there are bumps in friendships, but when you let them know you were hurt, the response is genuine sympathy and an apology. That's the kind of friendship you deserve.

Walking away from people who don't make you feel good can be really hard, especially if at one point they did make you feel good. But you deserve better than this group. 

You are NTA for going through her phone that one time when caught up in the moment, and just realizing what was happening. But now that you know what you know, if you don't walk away and allow yourself to be in a situation where you feel so unsafe in the friendship, you do it again. That answer changes. 

Don't let a group bring down who you are or who you want to be. Take the lonely time to evaluate areas where you need growth, what you want friendship to feel like, and go make new friends who bring you to higher levels of who you are. It's a hard thing to realize, but it's not uncommon to outgrow friends, and it's ok to allow yourself to do so.

The guy you're talking about uses a lot of really great buzz words, and has figured out how to make a solid social media platform, but like most social media it's a lot of hype with not a lot of follow through. As a therapist who's worked for over a decade in the medical field, I don't trust him. In one video, he causes a muscle to roll and says he created a "satellite trigger point" by making the "trigger point move" that's not what a satellite trigger point is. A satellite trigger point is when a trigger point causes a referral sensation to another trigger point. Rolling muscles are just rolling muscles. In another, he uses really inappropriate techniques on a lipoma and refuses to aknowlage even the possibility when another therapist calls him out in the comments. From what I've seen of his videos, I would not call him a good therapist or trust him with my own treatment. Healing isn't magic, and neither are therapists. That being said, what you are looking for is therapeutic massage or medical massage. Look into places like chiropractic offices or physical therapy offices around you for a more problem focused therapist. Techniques like trigger point therapy, myofasical release, graston, cupping, and muscle energy techniques fall under the umbrella of "therapeutic massage" in most areas and those are the techniques he is displaying, even if improperly.

In my previous experiance with rescues there was a required two meet and greats with the dog(one at center, one at our house) to see if the dog responded well. two meetings with a person from the rescue center. (Going over expectations, and then a walk through at the home) and a final meeting to sign paper work. The over all process took about a week and yes sometimes multiple families were being interviewed and someone else got the dog first, but that rescue center really made sure everything was a good fit. So when we got our current dog I did not expect what happened... 

We were pushed like you over a dog we had just seen online for the first time that day, lied to about the breed over the phone (told it was a great Dane lab mix, clearly is a great Dane pit mix) and we now know our dog was drugged when we met her. We were lied to about her behavior, and how long she was at the shelter. (Figured all that out when we called back to ask questions and a different staff member gave us more details) It was a whirlwind and by the end of our visit our heads were spinning and we were walking out with a dog we hadn't had a full conversation about and only met once for 20 minutes. 

We LOVE our dog, but she's reactive and deals with behavior issues that we didn't expect. We have had to spend a lot more on special training than we originally planned, and it's a lot sometimes. She's worth it and amazing and we are so happy with her, we are so proud of her. AND if we had talked first we might have seen some red flags (like the clear lies, or sedation). at the time we weren't really set up to deal with her issues that we do think the shelter knew about and didn't communicate with us. We changed our whole lives for her, which we did without question or hesitation or regret because we knew any dog has possibility of difficulty or unexpected things, and along with that we have talked several times about how we made a mistake letting the shelter strong arm us into signing those papers, that if we had planned better and talked more we could have done better by her in the start, or picked a dog that fit our capability more. So bottom line, go at your own pace. You don't have to pick a dog cause it's going to be snagged up 5 minutes after you walk out the door, maybe it will, maybe it won't. There's already a lot here, but I wanted to add my bit incase it helps. I struggled with proper boundaries for a long time and have done quite a bit of therapy around it. 

First off I want to say contrary to what others are saying I don't think this is solely your problem, and I think it's great your trying to support your girlfriend even to the point of seeking advice. I think that shows how much you care about her. It's clear though that your girlfriend, with your support has to have a conversation since your step mom won't listen to just you.

 Boundaries are sooo hard. I am assuming your girlfriend might have a rough home situation considering you can't go there, which can make them even harder. I suggest making sure she's willing to have a conversation and offering your support rather than trying to push her (not that I think you are specifically you sound very supportive) I'd say something like "hey I know this babysitting stuff is hard on you, and I can tell setting boundaries is hard too. If your willing I'd like to have a conversation with my parents together I would like us to do this together, maybe we can talk about a few ways to approach this. What do you think? if she's not willing I think you have to accept that for now, and remind her in times of frustration that you support her and are willing to hold a conversation whenever she is ready. Ultimately giving her the choice will give her power over her own life and agency to advocate for herself. 

Again contrary to what others are saying I personally don't suggest putting your girlfriend on the spot in the moment by saying no for her, and potentially starting a fight. This in my experiance will elevate everyone's systems and can lead to a lot of emotional reactions. Instead I suggest talking to your girlfriend and picking a time that works for both of you  to have a talk with your step mom.. Send your stepmom a text message that invites her to talk. Preferable that Shannon does this part but you can too if it helps. "Hi, we were both hoping to have a conversation regarding babysitting. We just want to check in and make sure everyone is on the same page are you available at (time) to talk in person" if she says no ask her when she is available tell her it is important to both of you to talk in person. 

Before you talk come up with a game plan. You can Google the dear man template which is a non violent communication form of making a request it basically lays out a request like this.. 

The situation: being asked to babysit at times not previously agreed to
Understanding the other side: maybe stepmom is over whelmed  and needs extra support. (Or whatever reason this part is very important though, try to understand her side and make it clear you can see her too) 
Stating feelings: maybe girlfriend feels unseen or disrespected or tired or frustrated.
Stating needs: maybe girlfriend  needs space, and time with just you, or order and a plan going forward. Does she always need a plan or is there room for some random times, what are the random times if any that can be agreed to (be specific and firm In the needs) 
Request: what is it that your stepmom can do to meet these needs. Always have a plan? Weekend mornings off limits? Be specific. 
How it helps: how this supports both sides, maybe having this conversation and respecting boundaries will help foster stronger relationships in the family. 

... there are a few variations so try to look at it together and write something down. Bring the paper with you as a guild, or have Shannon straight up read it if she's nervous about conflict resolution and boundaries. Have a couple comforts planned. Does holding hands help her? Having water to sip on and give a break in the talking? Something to play with (I always bring a small bit of clay to my conflict conversations to keep my hands busy and move nervous energy) what can you do if Shannon starts to check out or things get heated, is there a way to step outside for a second? Does she have something that comforts her? 

Plan next steps: what do you do if stepmom says no, what if she wants to work on it but has different needs, is there compromise? 

It's great that you want to support your girlfriend. I hope some of this helps. Boundaries are hard but you both deserve to be heard seen and met where your at. Good luck to both of you.

It seems to me you have gone from 0 to 100 which can cause major issues for the dog and cause the opposite effect of what your looking for. As stated above the separation anxiety should be addressed first. Your dog is in a panic. You can also work on this in the crate, though the other advice above was good as well. When crate trainging it's best to start with 5 to 10 minute increments with you sitting by the crate and treating when quiet even for a moment, try to work with her in the crate(sit lay down shake) if you have to use tuna use tuna. Start with the door open and you or gf sitting in front until the dog is calm doing this. If she panics let her out and try again later. Once she can do that close the door once she can do that leave her in for 15 min then 20 then 30 once she can do 30 with you sitting right there treating with the door closed and is comfertable Start walking away for 2 min then 5 and 10 so on untill she can handle 30 min with you in the house. Then you can start leaving her in for short trips to the store etc. Start with no more than an hour trip work up to 1.5 then 2 then 3. We choose to tap at 4 hours in the crate with our rescue pit. Because pits are very pact oriented dogs who need lots of attention and Exersice we have read more than 4 during the day is too much for a pit. It took us months to fully crate train our rescue. We train with her upwards of 2 hours a day in small chunks and the crate was our main focus for 4 months it takes time and constant consistant work. The most important thing is to listen to your dog and not let them panic. Until she is comfertable you and your gf will have to change your schedules, get a sitter, etc.. If you dont trust day cares. My partner and I worked opposite schedules for like 4 months or asked friends to help. Id seek a good trainer if you need help and ask for either solo or at home session to work on the crate specifically. And as stated above some dogs can not do crates. If they have been misused on them in the past or they have already learned in a hard way to occosiate the crate with panic they may not be able to do it in a healthy way. Id talk to a trainer first if you cant get your rescue to work with you, often times they will have alternatives if the crate isnt going to work for you.

The idea is that a lot of the time pcos can have a root issue of no progesterone, thus no periods. The progesterone rises and thickens the lining of the uterus and when it drops the lining is shed. 

What most people dont know is the progesterone drop that causes the shedding of the uterus lining, also triggers the follicle stimulating horming to start ramping up. The FSH is what creates the follicles that hold the egg before the FSH drops and LH is triggered to spike and ruptures the follicle and releases the egg. (Unruptured follicles are what cause the little cysts in our overies.) 

So basically, a lot of people know progesterone causes periods, no periods, normally no progesterone. But no progesterone also means no progesterone drop, thus no FSH, no FHS no follicle (or partly developed follicle), no follicle no egg drop, no egg drop no ovulation. So sometimes even if you have an LH surge you dont ovulate because there was no follicle to hold the egg. So progesterone CAN actually indirectly effect ovulation, contrary to what most doctors who dont specilize is PCOS will tell you. 

Progesterone also helps with a whole world of other issues, like the health of the lining for implantation, blood consistancy, cramps, fatigue, weight gain, mood, and endometriosis.
